evidence_contexts.source_text:
In some degenerate cases the label shift
and covariate shift assumptions can hold simultaneously.
### Label Shift

Label shift is the appropriate assumption here
because diseases cause symptoms.
### Label Shift Correction

Interestingly, in these cases,
it is often advantageous to work with methods
that flow from the label shift assumption.
*Label shift* describes the converse problem.

One nice thing about label shift is that
if we have a reasonably good model
on the source distribution,
then we can get consistent estimates of these weights
without ever having to deal with the ambient dimension.

Label shift is a reasonable assumption to make
when we believe that $y$ causes $\mathbf{x}$.
Synthetic: The package was rejected because of label shift on the sticker, not because of a data distribution issue.

source_payload.proposed_definition_en: distribution shift where the label distribution changes, typically under the assumption that labels cause the observed features.

evidence_contexts.source_text: Moreover, we remove the maximum pooling layer.

That is to say, using the $2\times 2$ maximum pooling layer,
we can still detect if the pattern recognized by the convolutional layer
moves no more than one element in height or width.

We can demonstrate the use of padding and strides
in pooling layers via the built-in two-dimensional maximum pooling layer from the deep learning framework.

Each NiN block is followed by a maximum pooling layer
with a stride of 2 and a window shape of $3\times 3$.

One VGG block consists of a sequence of convolutional layers,
followed by a maximum pooling layer for spatial downsampling.

More concretely,
each downsampling block consists of 
two $3\times3$ convolutional layers with padding of 1
followed by a $2\times2$ maximum pooling layer with stride of 2.

The basic building block of classic CNNs
is a sequence of the following:
(i) a convolutional layer
with padding to maintain the resolution,
(ii) a nonlinearity such as a ReLU,
(iii) a pooling layer such
as a maximum pooling layer.
We can construct the input tensor `X` in :numref:`fig_pooling` to [**validate the output of the two-dimensional maximum pooling layer**].
Synthetic: The maximum pooling layer of blankets on the bed made the room look untidy.

source_payload.proposed_definition_en: a pooling layer that outputs the maximum value within each local window, often for downsampling

evidence_contexts.source_text: At the current scale, the object detection model needs to predict the classes and offsets of $hw$ sets of anchor boxes on the input image, where different sets have different centers.
* Single shot multibox detection is a multiscale object detection model.

In a nutshell,
via its base network and several multiscale feature map blocks,
single-shot multibox detection
generates a varying number of anchor boxes with different sizes,
and detects varying-size objects
by predicting classes and offsets
of these anchor boxes (thus the bounding boxes);
thus, this is a multiscale object detection model.

For a predicted bounding box $B$,
the object detection model calculates the predicted likelihood
for each class.

Now we are ready to use such background
knowledge to design an object detection model:
single shot multibox detection
(SSD) :cite:`Liu.Anguelov.Erhan.ea.2016`.

We will design an object detection model
based on anchor boxes in :numref:`sec_ssd`.

In order to train an object detection model,
we need *class* and *offset* labels for each anchor box,
where the former is
the class of the object relevant to the anchor box
and the latter is the offset
of the ground-truth bounding box relative to the anchor box.

![As a multiscale object detection model, single-shot multibox detection mainly consists of a base network followed by several multiscale feature map blocks.](../img/ssd.svg)
:label:`fig_ssd`
Synthetic: Object detection is the task, while an object detection model is the trained network that performs it.

source_payload.proposed_definition_en: a model that detects objects in an image by predicting their classes and locations.

evidence_contexts.source_text:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{MSE} (\hat{\theta}_n, \theta) &= E[(\hat{\theta}_n - \theta)^2] \\
 &= E[(\hat{\theta}_n)^2] + E[\theta^2] - 2E[\hat{\theta}_n\theta] \\
 &= \mathrm{Var} [\hat{\theta}_n] + E[\hat{\theta}_n]^2 + \mathrm{Var} [\theta] + E[\theta]^2 - 2E[\hat{\theta}_n]E[\theta] \\
 &= (E[\hat{\theta}_n] - E[\theta])^2 + \mathrm{Var} [\hat{\theta}_n] + \mathrm{Var} [\theta] \\
 &= (E[\hat{\theta}_n - \theta])^2 + \mathrm{Var} [\hat{\theta}_n] + \mathrm{Var} [\theta] \\
 &= (\mathrm{bias} [\hat{\theta}_n])^2 + \mathrm{Var} (\hat{\theta}_n) + \mathrm{Var} [\theta].\\
\end{aligned}
$$
To learn the FM model, we can use the MSE loss for regression task, the cross-entropy loss for classification tasks, and the BPR loss for ranking task.
Perhaps the simplest metric used to evaluate estimators is the *mean squared error (MSE)* (or $l_2$ loss) of an estimator can be defined as

$$\mathrm{MSE} (\hat{\theta}_n, \theta) = E[(\hat{\theta}_n - \theta)^2].$$
:eqlabel:`eq_mse_est`
The MSE provides a natural metric, but we can easily imagine multiple different phenomena that might make it large.
MSE is always non-negative.
Synthetic: In a company dashboard, MSE could be an internal project code, not mean squared error.

source_payload.proposed_definition_en: Mean squared error; a non-negative metric or loss equal to the average squared difference between an estimate or prediction and the true value.
